candidateRows: Science can ultimately explain every real question because publicly testable evidence and mutually supporting scientific ideas reveal the fabric of reality without any evident terminal barrier.
This is the con side's opening answer to the motion and supplies its governing account of science, legitimate questions, evidence, and prospective explanatory completeness.

Atkins defines science as evidence-based public inquiry, distinguishes evidential questions from projected human concerns, and argues that sustained progress supports confidence that science will answer every genuine question.
Natural science cannot answer every meaningful question, scientism is logically self-defeating, and scientific and purposive explanations can coexist without competing.
This is the pro side's principal opening case, establishing limits on natural science and the central distinction between mechanistic and agent-purpose explanations.
Atkins's opening claim that science can in principle explain everything genuinely worth explaining.

Lennox accepts broad evidence-based inquiry while denying that natural science exhausts explanation, arguing that meaning, origin, destination, and agency require complementary forms of rational explanation.
The resurrection should be rejected because later religious testimony is not credible evidence and the immediate physical decay of a dead body makes natural reconstitution impossible.
The move directly challenges the central historical miracle offered for Christianity and tests whether religious claims can satisfy the debate's evidence-based explanatory standard.
Lennox's claim that Christianity is evidence-based and centrally supported by Jesus's resurrection.
Atkins contests both the historical support and physical possibility of the resurrection, treating it as an unsupported assertion rather than an event that can ground a religious explanation.
Science establishes natural regularities but cannot rule out resurrection, because an exceptional divine input need not violate the regularities governing what nature ordinarily does.
This supplies the pro side's core reconciliation of miracles with scientific law and directly defends the central Christian event against the con side's impossibility objection.
Atkins's contention that bodily decay makes resurrection impossible and that science can dismiss it.

Lennox argues that laws describe regular natural behavior rather than prohibiting an external agent, so recognizing normal regularity can identify an exception without alleging that natural law was broken.
Invoking an unrestricted divine agent is an intellectually lazy explanation because it replaces the difficult investigation of underlying biological, chemical, physical, and mathematical processes.
The move attacks the explanatory legitimacy of theism itself and contrasts divine agency with the layered, labor-intensive causal accounts supplied by scientific inquiry.
Lennox's claim that God can introduce a resurrection event into the natural regularities God created.

Atkins argues that divine attribution can accommodate any observation without uncovering a mechanism, whereas science earns explanatory satisfaction by tracing events through progressively deeper natural processes.
A mindless and unguided origin of human cognition undermines trust in the rational faculties required for science, whereas theism explains why minds can understand an orderly world.

This reverses the explanatory challenge by arguing that naturalism cannot securely ground scientific rationality while theism accounts for both an intelligible universe and minds capable of knowing it.
Atkins's charge that explanations involving God are speculative, lazy, and intellectually corrupt.

Lennox connects confidence in science to confidence in cognition, uses the analogy of an unguided computer to question naturalistic reliability, and presents theism as a stronger basis for rational inquiry.
Evolution can produce brains capable of extraordinary scientific understanding, although human intuition may remain limited even where mathematical science predicts phenomena with great precision.
This is the con side's substantive answer to the evolutionary reliability objection and distinguishes limits of human intuition from limits on successful scientific explanation.
Lennox's argument that unguided evolution undermines confidence in the rational faculties used to conduct science.

Atkins credits evolution and collaboration for human understanding, concedes possible cognitive limits, and argues that precise mathematical mastery can still count as understanding even without intuitive access.
The historical emergence of modern science is evidence that belief in a single rational creator supports an intelligible universe and explains the fit between nature and the human mind.
The move develops the positive explanatory case for theism beyond mere motivation, linking scientific origins, cosmic rationality, and human cognition in an inference to the best explanation.
Atkins's claim that religious belief may motivate achievement without providing evidence that God actually exists.

Lennox argues that creator belief was historically distinctive and scientifically generative, then treats that history as cumulative support for a worldview in which one rational source grounds world and mind.
A cosmic purpose is not a real evidential question because it merely projects temporary human purposes onto the universe, for which no corresponding evidence exists.
This directly addresses whether purpose belongs among the things worth explaining and supplies the con side's criterion for excluding ultimate-purpose questions from legitimate inquiry.
The challenge that dismissing questions science cannot answer, including human and cosmic purpose, is overly convenient.
Atkins distinguishes individual and ephemeral aims from an ultimate purpose of the universe and argues that extrapolating from the former to the latter lacks evidential warrant.

Christianity's historically grounded creation narrative makes purposeful human significance a coherent explanatory possibility rather than a meaningless question, even if its truth remains disputable.
The move answers the exclusion of purpose by presenting a rival worldview in which creation and human significance form a coherent historical metanarrative open to rational evaluation.
Atkins's claim that there is no evidence of cosmic purpose and that asking for it is an inappropriate extrapolation.

Lennox presents Christianity as more than abstract philosophy, connecting its creation claim to a large account of human significance and arguing that purpose remains intelligible and worthy of inquiry.
Christianity supplies an evidence-linked worldview in which natural laws, biological information, resurrection, and transformed lives point toward divine intelligence and personal meaning.
The move directly contends that scientific observations do not exhaust explanation and that Christianity adds rational, historical, and personally testable explanatory resources.
Atkins's preceding contention that there is no evidence for God and that religious explanations rest on an unsupported foundation.
After Atkins dismisses evidence for God, Lennox presents Christianity as a broad explanatory framework connecting intelligibility in nature with historical and experiential claims.
The laws of nature can be accounted for through impersonal principles of indolence, anarchy, and ignorance without positing a divine agent.
This is a direct naturalistic alternative to divine explanation for the order and lawfulness of the universe, addressing the debate's central explanatory dispute.
Lennox's argument that the rational structure and laws disclosed by science indicate an originating divine mind.
Atkins answers the appeal from natural law to God by outlining impersonal principles that he claims suffice to explain the laws science identifies.
The universe originated from no physical material but not from absolute nothing, because nonphysical divine mind is the fundamental creative source.
The move supplies the pro side's positive account of cosmic origin while arguing that Big Bang cosmology is compatible with, and suggestive of, creation.
Atkins's account in which absolute nothing changes into something without requiring a personal creative agent.
In the exchange over cosmic origins, Lennox distinguishes absence of physical matter from absence of all reality and connects a cosmic beginning to divine creation.
A universe can arise from nothing through the separation of balanced opposites, with total charge and energy summing to zero and science progressively simplifying the remaining problem.
This gives the con side's principal scientific account of how cosmic existence might emerge without God while acknowledging that the final mechanism remains unresolved.
Lennox's claim that a physical beginning requires an antecedent nonphysical divine mind rather than absolute nothing.
Atkins accepts that a beginning is possible and argues that balanced positive and negative quantities reduce the origin question to how nothing separated into opposites.
Balanced physical quantities do not amount to nonexistence, and naturalistic origin accounts commonly evade the problem by redefining nothing as something physical.
The reply challenges the conceptual foundation of the con side's origin account by separating net-zero measurements from the existence of an entire physical system.
Atkins's proposal that equal and opposite charge and energy make the universe equivalent to nothing at the aggregate level.
Lennox disputes the inference from balanced quantities to nothingness and argues that space-time and a physical system still require explanation despite net-zero properties.
No conceivable observation would rationally establish God, because even witnessing a resurrection should be treated as hallucination rather than supernatural intervention.
The move states the con side's epistemic standard for miracle claims and openly characterizes its atheistic conclusion as resistant to observational falsification.
Asked what could change his mind, Atkins says no candidate observation would do so because apparent supernatural events would always be less credible than cognitive error.
Christian belief is in principle revisable through historical and experiential counterevidence, while its cumulative support warrants continued commitment and scrutiny.
This contrasts the pro side's claimed openness to falsification with Atkins's declared immunity to contrary observation and grounds belief in cumulative considerations.
Atkins's admission that no evidence, including an apparently witnessed resurrection, could move him from disbelief.
Lennox answers that contrary historical explanations and defeaters for attributed experiences could prompt reconsideration, though he regards their cumulative force as substantial.
Morality can be illuminated scientifically as evolved behavioral infrastructure supplemented by humans' capacity to contemplate the consequences of their actions.
The move directly extends the claim that science explains reality into morality, one of the principal domains alleged to require a different kind of explanation.
In response to a question contrasting scientific facts with religious values, Atkins treats moral practices as evolved behavior refined by distinctively human reflection.
Science may describe moral behavior and consequences, but natural laws and evolutionary labels cannot generate prescriptive duties or furnish a scientific foundation for ethics.
The move identifies an explanatory boundary between facts and obligations, directly supporting the position that science cannot explain everything worth explaining.
Atkins's argument that evolutionary science, ethology, anthropology, and psychology can explain the roots and development of morality.
Lennox rejects the evolutionary account as insufficient for normativity, distinguishing scientific descriptions of nature from rules governing what people ought to do.
Human beings share a cross-cultural core of moral intuitions, which Lennox explains through humanity's creation as morally responsible beings in God's image.
The move provides a positive theistic explanation for widespread moral convergence while acknowledging shared practical judgments among believers and nonbelievers.
During discussion of how technology should be used, Lennox argues that common moral responses appear across cultures and worldviews and attributes this core to divine creation.
Human moral commonality arose through an evolutionary process favoring survival of both individuals and groups.
This supplies the naturalistic explanation for shared morality that competes directly with the claim that moral awareness reflects creation in God's image.
Lennox's claim that common moral judgments are explained by humans being made in the image of God.
The speakers agree that humans display a broadly shared moral core but dispute whether its explanatory source is divine creation or evolutionary group survival.
The Judeo-Christian legacy provides the indispensable foundation for Western human rights, institutions, and basic morality.
The move argues that secular evolutionary commonality does not adequately explain or sustain the normative inheritance underlying Western moral and political institutions.
Atkins's proposal that shared morality is adequately explained by a common evolutionary process supporting group survival.
After Atkins attributes common morality to evolution, Lennox appeals to an atheist intellectual's acknowledgment of Christianity's foundational role in Western moral institutions.
Atheistic societies cannot safely discard God while retaining a stable and adequate value for human beings.
It uses the experience of an avowedly atheistic political culture to argue that human dignity depends on more than a purely secular account of morality.
Atkins's assertion that people would be far better off living in an atheistic country.
The exchange turns from Christianity's cultural legacy to whether explicitly atheistic societies can preserve human value after eliminating belief in God.
As science advances, its explanations increasingly eliminate any need to invoke supernatural causes.
This is a direct statement of the science-explains-reality side's central thesis about explanatory progress displacing supernatural accounts.
Asked whether scientific discovery is moving toward or away from God's existence, Atkins gives a compact account of scientific progress as explanatory secularization.
Scientific progress has not substantially reduced belief in God, while dissatisfaction with materialism is renewing interest in God and meaning.
The response directly disputes the claim that scientific advance steadily removes God by appealing to scientists' beliefs, explanatory dissatisfaction, and worldwide religious growth.
Atkins's claim that continued scientific progress makes supernatural causes progressively less necessary.
Lennox answers Atkins's secularization thesis with historical survey claims, renewed interest in science and God, searches for meaning, and the global prevalence of theism.
Natural selection cannot explain the origin of life because evolutionary mechanisms can operate only after life already exists.
The move identifies a claimed boundary of evolutionary explanation at the origin of living systems, directly challenging scientific explanatory completeness.
Atkins's contention that natural selection is a single biological rule accounting for nearly everything in biology.
Following a comparison of biologists and physicists, Lennox challenges the breadth assigned to natural selection by separating biological development from life's initial emergence.
Christian belief can be rationally selected among competing religions by historically investigating their incompatible claims about Jesus's resurrection.
It answers the methodological objection that choosing Christianity among religions lacks a reliable rational method and links faith to assessable historical explanation.
Asked why he believes Christianity rather than another faith, Lennox treats Jewish, Muslim, and Christian resurrection claims as incompatible historical propositions open to inference.
Christianity is uniquely grounded in acceptance as a free gift through Christ rather than in earning acceptance by religious merit.
This provides Lennox's second substantive reason for distinguishing Christianity from other religions and explains its account of salvation, meaning, and divine relationship.
Lennox contrasts merit-based religious paths culminating in uncertain judgment with Christian salvation, where acceptance precedes and motivates the believer's subsequent life.
Science is humanity's uniquely successful route into reality and is capable of answering the great questions of existence.
The closing explicitly affirms science as the means of reaching reality and answering the great questions while portraying religious belief as an obsolete chrysalis.
Atkins closes by praising humanity's collaborative and open-minded scientific enterprise, its penetration of reality's fabric, and its movement beyond religion.
Science is valuable, but the personal God who makes a scientifically intelligible world possible is the deeper explanation.
The final response encapsulates the science-has-limits side by affirming science while locating its possibility, truth, and ultimate meaning in God.
Atkins's closing claim that science penetrates reality, answers all great questions of being, and supersedes religious belief.
Lennox's closing accepts the wonder of science but argues that its intelligible world depends on God, understood not as abstraction but as a person.
